 3 Deadlines Battery and EV Buyers Need to Know Before April 2027
 The battery rebate drops on 1 January, Treasury is weighing further cuts, and the EV tax break changes in April. What’s confirmed, and what to do now.

 Enter your postcode to see the solar, battery and EV rebates in your area 
 Show my rebates 
 More than 600,000 home batteries have been installed under the federal rebate since July 2025, and roughly 35,000 more are going in every month. That success is now the problem. With inflation at 4.3% and Treasury hunting for savings, the battery rebate and the EV tax break are both in the firing line.
 If you’re weighing up a battery or an electric vehicle , the next five months matter. Some changes are already locked in. Others are only proposals, and may never happen. Mixing the two up is how people either rush a decision they didn’t need to, or miss a deadline they did.
 Here are the three dates that matter, what’s confirmed, what isn’t, and what to do about each.
 Quick summary 
 December 2026 (proposed): Treasury is preparing options to scale back the battery rebate ahead of the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook. Nothing has been decided.
 1 January 2027 (confirmed): The federal battery rebate steps down by about 16% per kWh. A 25 kWh battery gets roughly $840 less.
 31 March 2027 (confirmed, not yet law): The last day to start a novated lease with the full FBT exemption on an EV costing more than $75,000. Cheaper EVs keep it until April 2029.
 December 2026: Treasury’s savings options (proposed) 
 This is the one making headlines, and the one with the least certainty. The Australian Financial Review has reported that Treasury is preparing options to scale back the $7.2 billion Cheaper Home Batteries Program ahead of the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook (MYEFO), due in December. Options reportedly on the table include a lower upfront discount and requiring batteries to join a virtual power plant (VPP) .
 Ministers have confirmed they’ve been asked to find savings across their portfolios, and the Prime Minister hasn’t ruled out means-testing the rebate. Energy Minister Chris Bowen continues to defend the scheme publicly.
 What this means in practice:
 Nothing has changed yet. The rebate rules in force today are the ones set in May.
 Any cut would be on top of the scheduled January step-down , not instead of it.
 Past changes came with notice. The May 2026 changes were announced in December 2025, five months ahead. There’s no guarantee of the same lead time, but a surprise overnight cut would be unusual.
 Expert tip 
 If you sign a battery quote now, check whether the price is conditional on the rebate amount at installation. A “subject to rebate” clause tells you who wears the risk if the rules change before your install date.
 1 January 2027: the battery rebate steps down (confirmed) 
 This one is locked in. Under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program, the rebate is calculated from a factor that falls every six months until 2030. On 1 January 2027, that factor drops from 6.8 to 5.7, cutting the rebate by about 16% per kWh. It falls again to 5.2 on 1 July 2027.
 Here’s what that means for common battery sizes, assuming a certificate price of around $37 after fees:
 Usable capacity Installed by 31 Dec 2026 Installed from 1 Jan 2027 Difference 
 10 kWh $2,516 $2,109 −$407 
 14 kWh $3,522 $2,953 −$569 
 20 kWh $4,428 $3,712 −$716 
 25 kWh $5,183 $4,345 −$838 
 30 kWh $5,711 $4,725 −$986 
 Two details matter here. First, the rebate is set by the date your system is installed and signed off, not the date you sign the quote. Second, installers are busy. October was the biggest month for rooftop solar this year, and December is always squeezed by holidays. If you want the current rate, book now and get the installation date in writing.
 Expert tip 
 Don’t let a December deadline push you into a bigger battery than you need. The difference between the two rates on a 14 kWh battery is about $570. Buying 10 kWh more than you’ll use costs far more than that.
 Book A Test Drive Today 
 31 March 2027: the EV tax break starts shrinking (confirmed, not yet law) 
 The Electric Car Discount lets you salary-package an eligible EV through a novated lease without paying fringe benefits tax (FBT). It’s worth thousands a year, and the higher your tax bracket, the more it’s worth. In May, the Government announced a three-stage wind-back after a Treasury review found the scheme had cost about $2 billion in its first three years, against an original estimate of $205 million over four.
 Period EVs costing $75,000 or less EVs over $75,000 (below the LCT threshold) 
 Until 31 March 2027 Full FBT exemption Full FBT exemption 
 1 April 2027 to 31 March 2029 Full FBT exemption 25% FBT discount 
 From 1 April 2029 25% FBT discount 25% FBT discount 
 So the 31 March 2027 deadline matters most if you’re looking at an EV over $75,000. If your car costs less, you have until April 2029. Vehicles above the fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold (currently around $91,000) don’t qualify at all.
 Expert reference 
 The Australian Taxation Office notes that existing leases won’t be affected by the changes, and that the measure is not yet law.
 Expert tip 
 The date that counts is when your lease arrangement starts, not when you order the car. With EV delivery times stretching for popular models, anyone targeting the March deadline should talk to their leasing provider now about what “commencement” means under their contract.
 What to do now 
 The right move depends on where you are.
 You have a battery quote in hand. Confirm the installation date in writing, ask whether the price is conditional on the rebate, and book before Christmas if you want the current rate. Don’t upsize just to chase the difference.
 You’re still deciding on a battery. Size it for your home first, using your evening and overnight usage. If the numbers stack up, acting before 1 January is worth around $400 to $1,000 depending on size. If they don’t stack up, no deadline changes that.
 You’re considering an EV over $75,000 on a novated lease. The full exemption ends on 31 March 2027. Talk to your employer and leasing provider now.
 You’re considering an EV under $75,000. There’s no rush. The full exemption runs until April 2029, and more affordable models keep arriving.
 You’re worried about means-testing. Nothing is confirmed. Watch for MYEFO in December, and remember that any new rules would likely come with notice.
 Expert tip 
 Treat the January step-down as the real deadline and MYEFO as the thing to watch. Planning around confirmed dates, rather than speculation, keeps you in control of the decision.
 Want the current rebate before it drops? 
 Compare quotes from accredited installers who can confirm an installation date before 31 December and show the rebate as a line item on your quote.

 Frequently asked questions 
 Is the federal battery rebate being cut? 
 A reduction on 1 January 2027 is already scheduled, cutting the rebate by about 16% per kWh. Beyond that, Treasury is reportedly preparing options to scale the program back ahead of December’s MYEFO, and the Prime Minister hasn’t ruled out means-testing. No further cuts have been announced or confirmed.
 How much does the battery rebate drop in January 2027? 
 The STC factor used to calculate the rebate falls from 6.8 to 5.7 on 1 January 2027. At a certificate price of around $37, that’s roughly $400 less on a 10 kWh battery, $570 less on 14 kWh and about $840 less on 25 kWh. Systems installed and signed off by 31 December keep the current rate.
 Will the battery rebate be means-tested? 
 It’s possible but not decided. The Prime Minister has declined to rule out means-testing for both the battery rebate and EV incentives, and ministers have been asked to find savings. Any change would most likely be announced at MYEFO in December or in the next budget, and past changes have come with several months’ notice.
 When does the EV FBT exemption end? 
 It winds down in stages. The full exemption applies to all eligible EVs until 31 March 2027. From 1 April 2027, EVs costing more than $75,000 get a 25% discount instead. From 1 April 2029, all eligible EVs get the 25% discount. Existing leases aren’t affected, and the ATO notes the measure isn’t yet law.
 Does the EV tax change affect my current novated lease? 
 No. The Australian Taxation Office says existing leases won’t be impacted by the changes. The new rules apply to arrangements that start after each phase begins, so a lease on a $90,000 EV that commences before 1 April 2027 keeps the full exemption for its term.
 Key takeaways 
 The battery rebate drops by about 16% per kWh on 1 January 2027. That’s confirmed, and set by your installation date.
 Treasury’s savings options for MYEFO in December are proposals, not decisions. Nothing has changed yet.
 The full EV FBT exemption ends on 31 March 2027 for EVs over $75,000, and in April 2029 for cheaper EVs.
 Existing leases are grandfathered, and the EV changes aren’t yet law.
 Plan around confirmed dates, size your battery for your home, and don’t let speculation drive the decision.
